title: Data in support of TNF inhibition in experimental rotator cuff tear mouse model
projectDescription: Musculoskeletal injuries related to the rotator cuff (RC) are frequent and account for up to 70% of shoulder pain problems. Lesions of the RC lead to weakness and pain (ref: Carr et al mfl) and untreated these lesions are acompanied by muscle degeneration modulated by inflammatory reactions that vary in intensity. Anti-inflammatory modalities such as NSAID and corticosteroids are commonly used as add ons to conservative treatment of RC tendon tears or RC tendon surgery, which are, however associated with  high failure rates. The aim was to study the impact that a conventional TNF inhibitor and a super selective TNF inhibitor (Anti-TNF treatment) has on soft tissue inflammation and bone constituent parameters/connective tissue in a rotator cuff tear model.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Groups of mice subjected to experimental SS tendon tear consisted of female mice that were allowed to survive for 5 days after surgery (6-7 mice/group), which is the time point where we previously have shown that post-surgical inflammation in the SS muscle peaks  The samples were prepared for Ultra Performance Liquid Chromatography (UPLC) tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) with a filter-based protein digestion protocol. The weight of each tissue sample was noted, fol-lowed by transfer of tissue sample to 1.5mL impact resistant tubes. 500µL of lysis buffer (LB) and ½ spoonful of beat beads were added to the tubes and the samples homogenized using a cooling bullet blender (Next Advance BB24-AU) for 2 times 5 minutes (min). Subsequent foam was removed by centrif-ugation and samples were denatured at 95? for 5 min. Protein concentration of each sample was then determined by A280 NanoDrop 1000 UV spectrophotometry (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA). Lysate volume containing 100µg protein was then calculated for subsequent preparation.  Volume containing 100µg protein was transferred to a 30kDa YM-10 tilted spinfilter and 200µL of LB was added. The spinfilters were then centrifuged at 14.000g until about 50µL was left in the spinfilter cup. 200µL of LB was then added again and centrifugation repeated. 200µL digestion buffer was then added to a final volume of 300µL followed by reduction and alkylation with 1:50 volume of tris(2-carboxy-ethyl)phosphine hydrochlorid (TCEP) 0.5M and 1:10 volume chloroacetamide 0.5M in triethylammonium bicarbonate buffer, vortexed and incubated in 30 minutes at 37?. Following incubation, 200µL diges-tion buffer was added and samples centrifuged. Samples were then protein digested by 200 mL digestion buffer containing 2 ?g trypsin in new 5mL collection tubes and stored in a plastic bag with a wet napkin at 37? overnight.  The next day following protein digestion, the spin filters were discarded and the collection tubes, containing the sample, were phase separated by adding 1,500µL of ethyl acetate and acidified by 20µL trifluoroa-cetic acid (TFA). The samples were vortexed and centrifuged for 1 minute, to obtain phase separation. The top phase containing the buffer was then extracted by pipetting. The process was repeated and the lower phase containing the sample peptides was dried in a vacuum centrifuge and stored at -80?. Prior to UPLC-MS/MS analysis, samples were resuspended in 20mL of suspension buffer, vortexed, lightly centrifuged and ultrasonicated for 2 min. LC-MS/MS analysis Before loading the sample preparations onto the MS, all samples were resuspended in reversed phase loading buffer containing 2% acetonitrile (ACN), 0.1% formic acid (FA) and 0.1% TFA. Samples were then vortexed and ultrasonicated for 1 min, followed by centrifugation for 1 min at 14,000g. Samples were analyzed by a Dionex RSLC Proflow nanoUPLC system, connected to a Bruker timsTOF mass spectrometer (Bruker,Bremen,Germany). For ionization, a NanoSpray ion source (Proxeon, Odense, Denmark) was used. The flow was 5µL per min for sample loading onto a trapping column (Acclaim PepMap100 C18 2cm, 100um ID; 5µm particle size column, Thermo Scientific). Flow rate of the nanoflow was 205nL/min for the peptide separation on the analytical column, a 75 cm Acclaim Pepmap RSLC, 75µ ID column connected with nanovipers. Picotip “Silicatip” emitter from New Objective was used for nano-electrospray. The buffers of the liquid chromatography system consisted of buffer A (0.1% FA) and buffer B (99.9% ACN, 0.1% FA). The gradient used was 5-35% buffer B over 88 min. The mass spectrometer system was operated in data-dependent acquisition mode. Mass range of m/z 350 to 2200 was acquired at a resolution of approximately 45,000 for each full scan. The mass spectrometer would acquire up to 2 MS/MS acquisitions on abundant peptide precursor ions, in each cycle. Precursor ions were isolated by employing a quadropole isolation window of 2.0 m/z and fragmented in a collision-induced dissociation collision cell dynamic collision energy,optimized for peptide fragmentation. Dynamic exclusion was set to 30 seconds.
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw output data was identified using MaxQuant version 1.6.0.1 with Andromeda search engine 7. The raw data was searched against a reference proteome of mus musculus (Proteome ID UP000000589, 16854 Entries) from UniprotKB database. As a cutoff, a false discovery rate (FDR) of 0.1% was used for both the protein and peptide level with the “match between runs” feature enabled. Fixed modification was set a carbamidomethylation. N-terminal acetylation and oxidation of methionine was set as variable modification. Sample list and LC-MS raw data summary is provided as excel file. All raw data as ip files of Bruker data. Search data based and search output provided as zip file of combined output
